newsitem.title: USA: Dole still on attack as Clinton takes a break.
newsitem.headline: Dole still on attack as Clinton takes a break.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
Republican presidential challenger Bob Dole put in a hectic day of travel through New Mexico, Kansas, Colorado and Kentucky on Friday while President Bill Clinton took a brief break from campaigning.
With two-and-a-half weeks left before Election day on November 5, Dole edged closer to Clinton in the latest Reuters tracking poll, in which he trailed by nine percentage points.

The poll showed previously lukewarm Republicans were finally rallying to the Dole ticket following Wednesday's second presidential debate, in which Dole sharply attacked the ethical standards of the Clinton administration.
Three other polls put the Republican challenger between 12 and 14 points behind, with Reform Party candidate Ross Perot stuck in single digits.
Clinton spokesman Joe Lockhart said internal polling by the campaign showed Clinton widening his lead after the debate in San Diego, California.
"The debate helped us," Lockhart said.

Dole appears to have decided he has nothing to lose by sharply escalating his attacks on Clinton's ethics. He came out on Thursday with a new accusation that the Clinton campaign was "money-laundering" foreign funds to finance his re-election bid.
"We're going to get tough," Dole said at a rally in Riverside, California, on Thursday. "You haven't seen anything yet."
Dole campaign manager Scott Reed on Friday issued a detailed statement addressed to Clinton and fleshing out the accusation.
"Some of your party's biggest contributors appear to have been Indonesian billionaires, South Korean companies, parishioners at Buddhist temples and foreign gardeners with green cards," Reed said.
"The questions that keep coming up are the same: where did the money come from? How was it funnelled to your campaign coffers? What did it buy?
"It's time to stop laundering foreign money and come clean with the American people," Reed said.
Republicans have attacked Clinton over reports that an Indonesian couple with ties to the financial conglomerate Lippo Group made a $425,000 donation to the Democratics.

House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich on Thursday called for an investigation into whether the Indonesian government won U.S. foreign policy favours in return for the money. Clinton officials have denied all such suggestions.
Lockhart responded to Reed's statement by citing three investigations of alleged campaign finance violations by the Dole campaign that he said were currently underway.
In one, a Massachusetts businessman who was a Dole campaign national vice chairman had admitted illegal contributions and was due to be sentenced soon.

The Capitol Hill newspaper "Roll Call" reported a review of federal election data showing more than two dozen members of Congress, mainly Democrats but also including Dole, received donations from individuals associated with the Lippo Group from 1988 to 1996.

In California on Thursday, Dole criticised a fundraiser attended by Vice President Al Gore last April at a Buddhist temple near Los Angeles, where members take vows of poverty but where Dole said Democrats got thousands of dollars.
"The next thing is they'll have a fundraiser at a homeless shelter," he said.
"That's called money laundering, and they've done so much of it they've got a laundromat next to the vice president's house in Washington, D.C," the Republican candidate said.
Clinton is due to leave on Sunday on his next campaign swing. It will take him to the hotly contested states of New Jersey, Ohio, Michigan and Florida.
In a sign of confidence, he also plans to raid Dole's Republican heartland with a trip to Alabama next week.
